vignette:
The Weight of Water

Marcus has been fishing the same coastal waters for thirty-eight years. He knows the tides by heart, can read the sky before the weather turns, and has built a reputation as one of the most reliable fishermen in the community. His hands are weathered and scarred from decades of nets and lines, but they're steady hands-the kind people trust. His wife, Elena, has packed his lunch for nearly every morning of their marriage.

Three years ago, their daughter Sophia, twenty-four years old, was struck by a car while crossing the street near her apartment in the city, two hours away. Marcus wasn't there. He was on his boat, checking nets in the early morning, when Elena's call came through. The details remain fragmented in his mind-something about the hospital, about critical injuries, about needing to come now.

The drive felt endless. Marcus kept seeing Sophia as a child, running along the dock, laughing. He kept thinking about the last conversation they'd had, something ordinary about her job, about whether she was eating enough. He can't quite remember what he'd said in response. When he arrived at the hospital, Sophia was already gone.

The funeral happened. People brought food. Time moved in a strange, numb way. Marcus went back to fishing because it was what he knew, what his body understood even when his mind didn't. But something fundamental had shifted.

Now, three years later, Marcus still wakes at three in the morning, his heart racing, drenched in sweat. Elena lies beside him, and he can feel her pretending to sleep, knowing he won't talk about it. He gets up, makes tea, and sits on the back porch watching the darkness until dawn. During these hours, his mind replays scenarios that never happened-conversations with Sophia he never had, ways he might have prevented the accident if he'd been there, if he'd insisted she move back home, if he'd driven her that morning instead of going to the boat.

On the water, Marcus finds it harder to concentrate. He's always been meticulous about safety, but now he second-guesses himself constantly. Did he check the engine properly? Is the weather changing? He's had two close calls with other boats-nothing serious, but they've shaken him. He's become hypervigilant in a way that exhausts him. His crew has noticed. They give him space, but he can see the concern in their eyes.

Elena tries to reach him. She suggests they go to the city to visit Sophia's apartment, to do something together. Marcus finds himself irritable with her, snapping over small things-a dish left in the sink, the way she's looking at him. He doesn't mean it. He loves her deeply, but there's a wall now, and he doesn't know how to dismantle it. Sometimes he wonders if Elena blames him for not being there, though she's never said so. He blames himself enough for both of them.

The guilt is the heaviest thing Marcus carries. Heavier than nets full of fish, heavier than the weight of the water itself. He thinks about Sophia constantly-not just her death, but all the moments he missed by being on the boat, all the times he chose the sea over being present. He wonders if she knew he loved her. He's certain she did, but certainty feels slippery now.

Marcus continues to fish. He still knows these waters. But the ocean that once felt like home now feels like the place that took him away from the one moment that mattered most.
